title: The Bag of Acid That Never Burns You
blurb: Your stomach holds acid strong enough to dissolve metal, and rebuilds its own lining every few days to survive it.

blocks.prompt: The Bag That Squeezes Your Lunch
blocks.text: Your stomach is a stretchy bag with strong muscles around it. When it is empty, it is about the size of your fist. When you eat a big meal, it stretches out to make room. Inside, your stomach makes acid. The acid is sour and strong. It helps break your food into a warm soup. The muscles squeeze and roll the food around for a few hours. Then the soup leaves through a little door at the bottom. Your stomach growls when it is empty. That is just air and juice sloshing around in a bag with nothing in it.

blocks.prompt: The Bag That Does Not Burn
blocks.text: Swallow a bite of apple and it does not fall into your stomach. It gets pushed. A tube called the esophagus squeezes it down, ring by ring, the way you squeeze toothpaste along a tube. That is why you could swallow while hanging upside down. Your stomach is waiting at the other end. It is a muscular bag shaped a bit like the letter J, tucked up under your left ribs. When it is empty it is about the size of your fist, and its walls are folded up like a scrunched sock. A big meal unfolds those folds and the bag stretches. Then the work starts. The stomach makes acid, and the acid is strong. It is more sour than lemon juice. The muscles squeeze and roll and mash until your bite of apple is a warm soup called chyme. This takes two to four hours. Here is the strange part. That acid could burn a hole in your stomach, but it does not. Your stomach coats itself in a thick layer of slippery mucus, and it builds itself a fresh lining every few days.

4.title: The Bag of Acid That Never Burns You
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Bag of Acid That Never Burns You

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Most of your gut has 2 muscle layers, the stomach has 3
Acid plus an enzyme called pepsin attacks protein
The pyloric sphincter is the exit door
Absorbing mostly happens later, in the small intestine
Acid kills most bacteria riding in on your food

blocks.prompt: The Mixing Room, Not the Fuel Tank
blocks.text: Most people assume the stomach is where food becomes fuel for the body. It is not. Almost nothing you eat is absorbed there. The stomach is a mixing room and a security gate, and the real absorbing happens later, in the small intestine. Here is what the stomach actually does. It stores. A meal you swallowed in fifteen minutes would overwhelm your intestine if it arrived all at once, so the stomach holds it and releases it slowly, in small squirts, through a ring of muscle called the pyloric sphincter. It mixes. Most of your gut has two layers of muscle. The stomach has three, running in different directions, which lets it churn food rather than just push it along. It attacks. Glands in the stomach wall pour out hydrochloric acid, strong enough to dissolve some metals, along with an enzyme called pepsin that starts tearing proteins apart. And it guards. Most bacteria that arrive on your food do not survive the acid bath. The obvious question is why the stomach does not digest itself. The answer is a truce. Other cells in the same wall release a thick, slippery mucus that clings to the lining and cancels the acid out right at the surface, before it can touch living tissue. Meanwhile the lining replaces its own cells every few days. Your stomach stays whole by rebuilding itself faster than it can be damaged. When that truce breaks, you get an ulcer.

notes: Before 1822, nobody knew what digestion was
Alexis St. Martin healed with a hole into his stomach

That proved digestion is chemistry, not grinding

blocks.prompt: The Man With a Window in His Stomach
blocks.text: On June 6, 1822, on Mackinac Island in Michigan, a shotgun went off by accident inside a crowded trading post. The blast hit a young French Canadian fur trapper named Alexis St. Martin in the side, from close range. An army surgeon named William Beaumont was fetched. He dressed the wound and expected St. Martin to be dead by morning. St. Martin did not die. Over the next two years the wound healed, but it healed wrong. Instead of sealing shut, the edge of the hole in his side fused to the edge of the hole in his stomach, leaving a permanent opening about the width of a finger. A small flap of tissue settled over it like a lid. Lift the flap and you were looking directly into a working human stomach. Beaumont saw an opportunity that had never existed before. In 1822 nobody actually knew what digestion was. The competing theories were that the stomach ground food up mechanically, or cooked it with body heat, or simply let it rot. Beaumont began tying pieces of food to a silk string, lowering them through the hole, and pulling them out at intervals to see what was left. He also drew off samples of gastric juice, dropped food into them in a cup, and set the cup aside, far from any body heat or grinding muscle. The food dissolved anyway. That one result ended the argument. Digestion was chemistry. The stomach was manufacturing a fluid that took food apart on its own. Beaumont ran roughly two hundred experiments across ten years and published them in 1833, founding the science of digestion more or less single handed. The rest deserves honesty. St. Martin was a poor man who could no longer work as a trapper, and Beaumont was both the doctor who saved him and the man who wanted his stomach. Beaumont hired him as a servant and later held him to a signed contract requiring him to submit to the experiments. St. Martin ran away more than once. He outlived Beaumont by twenty seven years. When he finally died, his family left his body out in the sun to spoil before burying it deep, so that no doctor would ever want to open him up again.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Stomach pH runs about 1.5 to 3.5
Helicobacter pylori hides in the mucus layer
Its urease enzyme makes ammonia to cancel acid
Barry Marshall infected himself on purpose in 1984
Warren and Marshall won the Nobel Prize in 2005
It carries roughly half the world's population

blocks.prompt: The Ulcer Was an Infection All Along
blocks.text: For most of the twentieth century, every doctor knew what caused stomach ulcers. Ulcers came from stress, from spicy food, from a hard-driving personality flooding the stomach with too much acid. Treatment meant bland diets, antacids, and sometimes surgery to sever the nerves that told the stomach to make acid at all. Patients improved, relapsed, and improved again, for years, sometimes for life. Nobody seriously proposed an infection, because everybody knew that nothing could survive in the stomach. The acid was too strong. That reasoning was clean, obvious, and completely wrong. In 1979 a pathologist in Perth, Australia, named Robin Warren was studying samples of stomach lining under a microscope and kept noticing curved bacteria sitting right on the tissue, always clustered near the inflamed parts. He was told he was seeing contamination. He kept noticing them anyway. A young trainee named Barry Marshall was the one person willing to take the observation seriously, and together they tried to grow the organism in the lab. Every attempt failed. Then, over a long Easter weekend in 1982, a batch of culture plates was left in the incubator for five days instead of the usual two. The bacterium was simply slow. Colonies were waiting when the lab reopened. The organism is now called Helicobacter pylori, and it defeats the acid in two ways. It corkscrews down through the mucus layer to the wall beneath, where conditions are close to neutral, and it manufactures an enzyme called urease that splits urea into ammonia. Ammonia is alkaline. The bacterium moves inside a small cloud of chemistry it makes for itself, like a diver carrying a bubble. Finding a bacterium is not the same as proving it causes a disease, and this is where the story becomes famous. The standard proof required infecting an animal and reproducing the illness, and the animals Marshall tried would not cooperate. So in 1984 Marshall took a broth of Helicobacter pylori cultured from a patient and drank it. Within days he was nauseated, vomiting in the mornings, and his breath had turned foul. A camera passed into his stomach showed the lining red and inflamed. He had deliberately given himself gastritis, the condition that precedes an ulcer, and then he cured it with antibiotics. The medical world still took about ten years to change its mind. Habit is not evidence, but for a long time it behaves like evidence. Warren and Marshall were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2005. An ulcer that once meant a lifetime of bland food and possible surgery is now usually cured in roughly two weeks with a course of antibiotics. Helicobacter pylori also turned out to cause most stomach cancer, and it lives quietly in the stomachs of about half the people on Earth. The stomach is worth understanding on its own terms. It is worth understanding for this, too. The wrong answer held for a century not because anyone lied, and not because the evidence was hidden in some unreachable place. It held because a reasonable assumption, that nothing survives in acid, was never actually tested.
